rationale: The BOOK ENTRY defines 'the way' as covenant conduct — the walk — and prints Jeremiah 6:16 and Matthew 7:14 as its warrant. Both cited texts are conduct texts on their face: Jeremiah 6:16 commands standing in the ways, asking for the old paths and the good way, and 'walking therein,' with the refusal expressed as 'we will not walk therein'; Matthew 7:14 contrasts two ways with two ends, a figure the common interpretation itself classifies as the well-attested 'two ways' moral tradition. The Hebrew derek (from 'to tread') and Scripture's first definition of 'the way of the LORD' (Genesis 18:19, 'to do justice and judgment') independently ground the conduct sense, and 2 Peter 2:21 lays 'the way of righteousness' beside 'the holy commandment.' The strongest counter — 'the way' as a christological title naming Jesus himself as the exclusive means of access (John 14:6) — cannot account for the Old Testament and moral-tradition usage the entry cites without splitting the term into unrelated senses, whereas the book's core explains John 14:6 without remainder: Jesus bears the title as covenant-conduct walked perfectly ('the road made by His own treading'), and Paul's own defense of 'the Way' in Acts 24:14 ('believing all things which are written in the law and in the prophets') fits the conduct reading better than a purely titular one. The entry's core identification is therefore the best-supported explanation of the printed evidence, and nothing printed in the entry itself goes beyond that identification.
book_core_identification: 'The way,' as a biblical symbol, denotes covenant conduct — the manner of life or walk measured by God's covenant standard — rather than primarily a titular name for Christ as a means of access; Christ is 'the way' as that covenant conduct embodied and walked perfectly.
book_secondary_elaborations: The apposition '— the walk' glossing conduct as the biblical figure of walking (directly carried by Jeremiah 6:16's 'walk therein').
chapter_only_objections: The claim that prosphatos in Hebrews 10:20 should be rendered 'freshly slain' against every major translation's 'new' is a chapter-level philological argument not asserted in the entry.
The claim that 'the Way' in Acts 'was not a new religion' but old covenant-conduct walked in light of Messiah is a chapter-level historical thesis beyond the glossary definition.

The identification of the flaming sword of Genesis 3:24 with the word of God via Ephesians 6:17, and the shamar reading as 'preserving' rather than 'barring' the way, are chapter-only typological steps.
The equation 'thy law is the truth' (Psalm 119:142) as the controlling definition of 'the truth' in John 14:6 is a separate term's argument, not printed in this entry.
The door/doorpost typology (Deuteronomy 11:20 with Exodus 12) identifying Christ as the door marked by word and blood is a chapter-only elaboration.
The derek/mesillah (way vs. highway) distinction and the beast/lion decoding of Isaiah 35:8-10 are chapter-only supporting arguments.
strongest_counter_interpretation: 'The way' is primarily a christological title: Jesus Christ himself as the sole path or means of access to God the Father (John 14:6; Hebrews 10:19-20), with the Acts usage ('the Way' as the movement's name) presupposing that titular sense; conduct language in the Old Testament and Matthew 7:13-14 is background or secondary rather than the symbol's content.
counter_core_identification: 'The way' names the person of Christ as the exclusive route of access to God, not a pattern of covenant conduct.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that 'the way' symbolically denotes conduct; it asserts the term's core content is Christ's person as means of access, so that defining the glossary term as 'covenant conduct' misstates what the symbol is, reducing John 14:6 to an ethical pattern rather than a claim about who Jesus is.
counter_case: John 14:6 explicitly identifies the way with a person ('I am the way') and attaches an exclusivity clause ('no man cometh unto the Father, but by me') that reads most naturally as personal mediation, not a conduct standard.
Hebrews 10:19-20 calls Christ's flesh the 'new and living way' into the holiest — access language, not ethics language.
Acts repeatedly uses 'the Way' absolutely as the movement's name (Acts 9:2; 19:9, 23; 22:4; 24:14, 22), which mainstream scholarship ties to the christological title.
Isaiah 40:3 / Mark 1:2-3 apply 'prepare the way of the Lord' to Jesus, supporting a way-of-the-Lord's-coming sense rather than a conduct sense.
Defining the term as conduct risks flattening the passage's soteriology into moralism, a move the dominant tradition resists.
book_explanatory_advantages: Both texts actually printed with the entry (Jeremiah 6:16; Matthew 7:14) are unambiguous conduct texts: 'the good way, and walk therein' and the narrow way that 'leadeth unto life' — the counter must treat the entry's own citations as secondary background.

Scripture's first definition of 'the way of the LORD' (Genesis 18:19: 'to do justice and judgment') states the conduct sense outright, matching the book's stated method of letting Scripture's own definitions hold uniformly.
The etymology of derek (to tread) and the pervasive 'walk' idiom across Torah, Psalms, and Prophets carry the conduct sense as the established pattern across independent witnesses.
2 Peter 2:21 places 'the way of righteousness' in apposition to 'the holy commandment,' a New Testament confirmation of the conduct sense.

The book's core explains John 14:6 rather than evading it: Jesus is 'the way' as covenant conduct embodied and walked perfectly, which also explains why the exclusivity clause says 'unto the Father' and why Hebrews grounds the 'living way' in his flesh.

It explains Paul's defense of 'the Way' in Acts 24:14 as 'believing all things which are written in the law and in the prophets' — a conduct-and-covenant self-description the titular reading leaves unmotivated.
It unifies OT and NT usage under one symbol instead of positing a semantic break between the wisdom 'way' and the Johannine 'way.'
counter_explanatory_advantages: The counter matches the dominant homiletical reading of John 14:6 as personal mediation and exclusivity.
Hebrews 10:19-20's access-into-the-holiest imagery sits naturally with a means-of-access reading.
The absolute Acts usage as a proper name is most simply glossed as shorthand for following Jesus who is the way.
decisive_sources: Jeremiah 6:16 (printed with the entry: the good way is something one walks in)
Matthew 7:14 (printed with the entry: two ways as two manners of walking with two ends)
Genesis 18:19 ('keep the way of the LORD, to do justice and judgment' — Scripture's first definition of the phrase)
2 Peter 2:21 ('the way of righteousness' // 'the holy commandment')
Acts 24:14 (Paul defines 'the Way' as believing all things written in the law and the prophets)
John 14:6 with Hebrews 10:19-20 (accounted for by the book as conduct embodied in a person, so not counter-evidence)
unresolved_objections: The personal, exclusive force of 'no man cometh unto the Father, but by me' retains a mediatorial dimension that the conduct definition captures only through the book's embodiment thesis; a reader could still hold that the Johannine title carries more than covenant conduct, though this does not defeat the conduct sense the printed citations establish.
